n: Sarah dies at 127. She is the only woman in the Bible whose age at death is recorded—a mark of her honored place as mother of the covenant people.

f.w: an hundred and seven and twenty years
f.g: 127 years. Isaac would have been about 37.

n: Sarah dies in Hebron, and Abraham mourns and weeps for her. Scripture honors genuine grief; faith does not erase sorrow.

f.g: “City of Arba” (or “city of four”), an older name for Hebron.

n: Abraham rises from mourning to arrange a burial, approaching the Hittites who controlled the land.

f.g: Hittites—local people descended from Heth, son of Canaan (10:15).

n: Abraham admits he is a foreigner without land. Though God promised him all Canaan, he must ask to buy a burial plot.

f.g: A resident alien without property rights.
A respectful way of referring to burial.

n: The Hittites reply to Abraham’s request.

f.g: The local Hittite community, acting as a town council.

n: With elaborate courtesy, the Hittites call Abraham “a mighty prince” and offer him any tomb he likes. Their polite words open the bargaining.

f.g: Literally “a prince of God”—a highly respected person.
Tombs.

n: Abraham bows respectfully to the local people, showing humility and good manners.

f.g: A customary gesture of respect.

n: Abraham asks the council to speak to Ephron on his behalf—a formal, public negotiation.

f.g: Intercede for me; plead on my behalf.

n: Abraham names the property he wants—the cave of Machpelah at the edge of Ephron’s field—and insists on paying full price, so the purchase will be permanent and legal.

f.g: Machpelah may mean “double.” The traditional site is in Hebron today.

f.w: as much money as it is worth
f.g: The full price.

n: Ephron answers publicly, in the hearing of all the men at the city gate, where legal business was done.

f.g: In the hearing of.

n: Ephron offers to give the field and cave as a gift. In that culture this was likely a polite opening rather than a real gift.

f.g: Ephron offers the whole field, not just the cave—which may include obligations of ownership.

n: Abraham bows again before the people.

f.g: Abraham maintains courteous respect throughout.

n: Abraham politely refuses the gift and insists on paying. A gift could later be disputed; a purchase could not.

f.w: I will give thee money for the field

n: Ephron responds to Abraham’s offer.

f.g: The negotiation reaches its decisive point.

n: Ephron names a price of 400 shekels—“what is that between friends?” The price was quite high, but Abraham does not haggle.

f.g: About 10 pounds (4.5 kg) of silver—a large sum. Jeremiah later bought a field for 17 shekels (Jeremiah 32:9).

n: Abraham weighs out the full amount publicly, using the standard merchants’ weight. Coins did not yet exist, so silver was weighed.

f.g: Silver was weighed on scales before coins were invented.
By the standard weight accepted by traders.

n: The property is legally transferred, including the field, the cave, and every tree within its borders. The detailed list reads like a real ancient deed.

f.g: Legally confirmed; deeded.

n: The sale is confirmed before witnesses at the city gate. Abraham now legally owns his first piece of the promised land.
Abraham buries Sarah in the cave. Abraham, Isaac, Rebekah, Leah, and Jacob are later buried there too.

f.w: the cave of the field of Machpelah

n: The chapter ends by repeating that the field and cave were Abraham’s burial property. His small piece of land is a down payment on God’s larger promise.
